title: Measuring Stars: Distance, Brightness, the HR Diagram

cards.h: How far is a point of light?
cards.b: A star's brightness mixes two things: how powerful it really is, and how far away. To learn anything, astronomers must separate them. Measuring distance is the key step, and a chain of methods, the cosmic distance ladder, builds it from the nearest stars to the edge of the universe.

Hold a finger out and blink each eye: the finger jumps against the background. In the same way, a nearby star shifts slightly against distant stars as Earth moves around the Sun. The shift angle is its parallax. Friedrich Bessel first measured it in 1838 for 61 Cygni.

A star with a parallax of 1 arcsecond is 1 parsec away, about 3.26 light-years. The nearest star system, Alpha Centauri, is 4.37 light-years away, and its faintest member, Proxima Centauri, 4.24. The Gaia satellite has measured parallaxes for nearly two billion stars.

Luminosity is a star's true power output. Apparent brightness is how bright it looks from here. Light spreads over a sphere, so brightness falls with the square of distance: twice as far, a quarter as bright (inverse-square law).

Astronomers use magnitudes: a lower number means brighter, and 5 magnitudes equals a factor of 100 in brightness. Absolute magnitude is the brightness a star would have at 10 parsecs, so stars can be compared fairly.

Beyond a few thousand light-years parallax fails. We then use objects of known luminosity. Henrietta Leavitt found in 1912 that Cepheid variable stars pulse at a rate linked to their luminosity: slower pulses mean brighter stars. Time the pulse, know the true brightness, compare to apparent brightness, get distance. This ladder rung let Hubble measure Andromeda's distance in 1924.

Plot stars by temperature (colour) against luminosity and they do not scatter: they fall into groups. This is the HR diagram (Hertzsprung 1911, Russell 1913).

  • Main sequence: a diagonal band holding about 90 percent of stars, including the Sun, all fusing hydrogen.
  • Red giants: cool but huge, so bright.
  • White dwarfs: hot but tiny, so faint.

On the main sequence, position tells mass. Heavy stars are hot, blue and extremely bright but live short lives (millions of years). Light red dwarfs are dim but live for trillions of years. Luminosity rises roughly as mass to the power 3.5. The Sun is a middle-ranking star with a ten-billion-year life.

Each rung of the distance ladder is calibrated by the one below: parallax calibrates Cepheids, Cepheids calibrate supernovae. Independent methods agree to a few percent, and Gaia has tightened the bottom rung.

• 'The brightest-looking star is the closest or the biggest.' It may just be powerful, or near.
  • 'A larger magnitude means brighter.' It is the opposite.
  • 'Stars on the HR diagram are moving along it all the time.' They move over millions to billions of years, not days.

Vainu Bappu, builder of the Kavalur observatory, with Olin Wilson found in 1957 the Bappu-Wilson effect: the width of a calcium emission line in cool stars tells how luminous they are, giving a new distance tool. The Vainu Bappu Telescope (2.34 m) in Tamil Nadu is named after him. Meghnad Saha's work (1920) connected spectral type to temperature, which underpins the HR diagram.

• Parallax gives distances to nearby stars; Cepheids extend the ladder.
  • Brightness falls with distance squared; lower magnitude is brighter.
  • The HR diagram groups stars by temperature and luminosity.
  • Mass sets a star's position and lifetime.

Think about it: (1) Why do massive stars die sooner despite having more fuel? (2) Why can't parallax measure distance to other galaxies?
